opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me, a world model is best defined by what it lets you do. At its core, it's a model that can predict how the world will evolve, especially in response to actions. You give it the current state of the world, maybe a camera view, some sensor readings, and an action, like a robot moving its arm or a car turning left. It tells you what happens next.

Why is that useful? I think there are three main things.

The first is simulation and data generation. Physical AI, things like robots and autonomous vehicles, has a data problem. You can't easily collect millions of hours of a robot failing to pick up a cup, or a car in a near-crash at night in the rain. A good world model lets you generate those scenarios synthetically, at scale, with a lot of diversity. So it becomes a kind of data engine for training policies.

The second is evaluation. Before you deploy a policy on a real robot or a real car, you want to know how it will behave. Testing in the real world is slow, expensive, and sometimes dangerous. If your world model is faithful enough, you can roll out the policy inside the model and get a meaningful signal about whether it works.

The third, and I think the most exciting long term, is planning and decision-making. If an agent has a world model inside it, it can imagine: "If I do this, what happens? If I do that instead?" It can search over possible futures before acting. That's a lot closer to how humans reason about the physical world. We don't just react. We mentally simulate.

So I'd define a world model as a learned simulator of the world that's conditioned on actions. Its value comes from serving as a data generator, an evaluator, and eventually a planner for physical AI. Video generation is a big part of how we build these today, because video is such a rich record of how the world works. But a pretty video isn't the goal. The goal is whether the model actually helps an agent act better in the real world.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. The way I think about it, a world model is a model that can simulate the world. You give it the current state of the world, you give it an action, and it tells you what happens next. That's the core idea: a predictor of the future, conditioned on what an agent does.

Why is that useful? The simplest answer is that if you can simulate the world, you don't have to go out and run every experiment in the real world. Think about a robot or an autonomous vehicle. Collecting real data is slow, expensive, and sometimes dangerous. You can't crash a car ten thousand times to learn how not to crash. But if you have a good world model, you can put the robot or the car inside the simulation, let it try things, let it fail, and learn from those failures without any real-world cost.

So in terms of what it's useful for, I see three main things.

First, it's a data engine. You can generate synthetic data, including rare cases and edge cases that are hard to capture in reality. A truck losing a tire on the highway, a child running out from behind a parked car. These are things you want your system to handle but will almost never see in your training set.

Second, it's a policy evaluator. Before you deploy a policy to a physical robot, you want to know how it behaves. The world model lets you run it through many scenarios and check. It becomes a testbed.

Third, and this is the more ambitious direction, the world model can become the foundation for the policy itself. If a model deeply understands physics, object permanence, how things move and interact, that understanding is exactly what an embodied agent needs. The agent can plan by imagining the consequences of its actions before taking them. That's very close to what humans do. Before you reach for a glass, you already have a sense of what will happen.

I'll add one more thing. People sometimes equate world models with video generation, and there's overlap, but they're not the same. A video model is optimized to look good to a human. A world model has to be physically faithful. If the simulation looks beautiful but the ball falls through the table, it's useless for a robot. So for me, the defining question is not "does it look realistic," it's "can an agent trust it to learn from." That's how I define usefulness.

r001.rationale: It defines a world model as predicting what happens next given the current state and an action.

r002.rationale: It discusses predicting outcomes and simulating events, but does not identify explaining why an event happened as a purpose.

r003.rationale: It says a world model can understand physics, but does not characterize physics as building world models to understand how the world works.

astra-6.text:
I think a useful way to define a world model is as a model that lets you predict how the world will evolve, including in response to your actions. Given what you observe now, if you take a particular action, what happens next?

That’s useful because it allows you to reason about different possibilities before acting. For a robot, for example, you could ask, “If I move my arm this way, will I successfully pick up the object, or will I knock it over?” A world model lets you simulate those possibilities and use the predictions to choose an action. So the key is not just generating something that looks realistic; it’s making predictions that are useful for decision-making.

That makes it useful for planning. Instead of trying every action in the real world, an agent can imagine different possibilities, compare their consequences, and decide what to do. So the key is not just generating something that looks realistic. It’s predicting the consequences that matter for the task.
